paragraphs.source_en: Dokusen said, “You see, human beings have changed just that much between the old days and the present. The old days were an age when anything could be done so long as there was an order from above; the age that follows is one in which things appear that cannot be done even by command from above. The world today is such that, whether one be Your Highness or Your Excellency, it is no longer possible to bear down upon another person’s dignity beyond a certain point. To put it more strongly, in today’s society the more power the other party has, the more unpleasant the oppressed party finds it, and the more fiercely he resists. So the present differs from the past: it is an age of the new phenomenon that a thing is hard to accomplish precisely because it is commanded from above. In our age, many things that would have been almost unimaginable to people of the past have come to pass as perfectly reasonable. The changes in society and human feeling are indeed exceedingly strange. As for Meitei’s chronicle of the future just now, one may certainly call it a joke, but if we take it as an explanation of the tendencies to come, is there not much in it that deserves serious study?”

paragraphs.source_en: Meitei said, “When I have been granted so rare a sympathetic friend, I naturally feel compelled to continue my chronicle of the future. Just as Dokusen has so eloquently said, in today’s world anyone who tries to force his way through by sheltering under governmental authority, or by relying on two or three hundred bamboo spears, is an obstinate relic behind the times, like a man in a palanquin frantically trying to race a train. Such people are the very source of unreason, a Chohan-sensei of usurious black-market loans. So with people of that sort it is enough simply to sit quietly and watch their methods at work. My chronicle of the future is not concerned with such makeshift little problems before our eyes; it is a social phenomenon bearing on the destiny of all humanity. If, after deep reflection, I survey the tendencies of present civilization and divine the course of the distant future, marriage will become impossible. Do not be alarmed, gentlemen. The reason marriage will become impossible is this: as I said earlier, the present world is a society centered on individuality; in the days when a household was represented by its head, a district by its magistrate, and a country by its lord, no one except the representative possessed any personality at all. Even if they had any, it was not acknowledged. That state of affairs suddenly changed with a great clatter, and every living being began to assert his individuality; whoever one looked at, people came to behave as though they were declaring, you are you and I am I. If two people meet on the road, each thinks in his heart, if you are a human being, then I am one too, and they pass each other while inwardly buying a quarrel; thus the individual has grown strong. In other words, because individuals have grown equally strong, individuals have also grown equally weak. Insofar as it has become difficult for others to injure one, the individual has certainly grown strong. But insofar as one can no longer readily lay hands on another, he has plainly become far weaker than in the past. To grow strong is of course pleasing, but no one is grateful to grow weak; therefore, while one clings to one’s strong point and refuses to let another violate so much as a single hair, one also wants, by force if necessary, to enlarge one’s weak point and infringe on another by even half a hair. When things come to this, there is no space left between person and person, and merely living becomes exceedingly cramped. Each tries to expand himself as far as possible, swelling almost to the bursting point, and goes on living in endless torment. Because it is so painful, people seek in all sorts of ways some margin between one individual and another. Thus, tormented by suffering of their own making, the first device people contrived in the midst of that distress was the system of parents and children living apart. In Japan, just go and look deep in the mountains! Whole households, however many people they contain, live together under one roof; there is no individuality to assert, or if there is, no one asserts it, and so they manage to go on living together. Civilized people, however, are not like that. Even between parents and children, each must press his own will upon the other as far as possible, or he will lose out; therefore, in order to preserve the safety of both sides, they must inevitably live apart.
